posts.post_content: Which of the following diseases is classified among the "vesicular diseases" affecting livestock?

_aimcq_options.text: Foot-and-mouth disease
Coccidiosis
Anthrax
Rabies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is the classic member of the vesicular disease group, characterized by vesicle formation on the mouth, feet, and teats.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Rabies: A neurotropic viral disease with no vesicular lesions.
  • C. Anthrax: A bacterial (Bacillus anthracis) disease, not classified as vesicular.
  • B. Coccidiosis: A protozoal intestinal disease, unrelated to vesicular lesion classification.

posts.post_content: Besides FMD, which other disease must be differentiated as it also produces vesicular lesions in livestock?

_aimcq_options.text: Blue tongue
Rinderpest
Rabies
Vesicular stomatitis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vesicular stomatitis is a key differential for FMD, since both produce oral/foot vesicles and are clinically indistinguishable without laboratory testing.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Blue tongue: Causes oral erosions/haemorrhages but is not classified within the primary vesicular disease differential group in the same way as vesicular stomatitis.
  • B. Rinderpest: A morbillivirus systemic disease causing necrotic stomatitis, not classified as vesicular.
  • C. Rabies: A neurotropic disease with no oral vesicular lesions.

posts.post_content: Modern viral taxonomy classifies viruses primarily based on:

_aimcq_options.text: Colour of culture plaques exclusively
Host species affected exclusively
Nucleic acid type, capsid symmetry, and presence/absence of envelope
Geographic origin exclusively

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Viruses are classified primarily by nucleic acid type (DNA/RNA), capsid symmetry, and envelope status, along with genome structure and replication strategy.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Host species affected exclusively: Host range is a descriptive feature but not the primary basis of formal viral taxonomic classification.
  • A. Colour of culture plaques exclusively: Not a basis for viral classification.
  • D. Geographic origin exclusively: Not a basis for formal viral taxonomic classification.

posts.post_content: Foot-and-mouth disease virus belongs to which viral family?

_aimcq_options.text: Poxviridae
Paramyxoviridae
Picornaviridae
Herpesviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

FMD virus belongs to Picornaviridae (genus Aphthovirus), a small, non-enveloped RNA virus with multiple serotypes (O, A, C, SAT1-3, Asia1).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Poxviridae: The family for pox diseases (e.g. lumpy skin disease, orf), not FMD.
  • D. Herpesviridae: The family for herpesvirus diseases (e.g. IBR, MCF), not FMD.
  • B. Paramyxoviridae: The family for morbilliviruses (rinderpest, PPR, CDV), not FMD.

posts.post_content: Immunity to one FMD virus serotype (e.g. O) provides:

_aimcq_options.text: Protection only against serotype Asia1
No cross-protection against other serotypes (e.g. A, C, SAT, Asia1)
Enhanced susceptibility to all other serotypes
Complete lifelong cross-protection against all serotypes

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Immunity to one serotype provides no cross-protection against the other FMD serotypes, requiring multivalent vaccines matched to circulating strains in a region.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Complete lifelong cross-protection against all serotypes: Incorrect — FMD serotypes are antigenically distinct with no meaningful cross-protection.
  • A. Protection only against serotype Asia1: Incorrect — even this specific claim is not accurate; the general principle is no cross-protection between any of the distinct serotypes.
  • C. Enhanced susceptibility to all other serotypes: Incorrect — the correct concept is a lack of protection, not increased susceptibility, following exposure to another serotype.

posts.post_content: Vesicular exanthema of swine, another member of the vesicular disease differential group, is caused by a virus of which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Rhabdoviridae
Picornaviridae
Caliciviridae
Reoviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vesicular exanthema of swine is caused by a calicivirus (Caliciviridae), distinct from FMD's picornavirus and vesicular stomatitis's rhabdovirus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Picornaviridae: The family for FMD virus, not vesicular exanthema of swine.
  • D. Reoviridae: The family for orbiviruses like bluetongue/AHS, not vesicular exanthema.
  • A. Rhabdoviridae: The family for vesicular stomatitis virus (and rabies), not vesicular exanthema of swine.

posts.post_content: Vesicular stomatitis virus, a key FMD differential, belongs to which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Caliciviridae
Coronaviridae
Picornaviridae
Rhabdoviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Vesicular stomatitis virus belongs to Rhabdoviridae (the same family as rabies virus), transmitted by insect vectors (sandflies, black flies).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Picornaviridae: The family for FMD virus, not vesicular stomatitis virus.
  • A. Caliciviridae: The family for vesicular exanthema of swine virus, not vesicular stomatitis.
  • B. Coronaviridae: The family for coronaviruses (e.g. enteric coronavirus, IBV), not vesicular stomatitis.

posts.post_content: Rinderpest virus belongs to which viral family and genus?

_aimcq_options.text: Picornaviridae, genus Aphthovirus
Paramyxoviridae, genus Morbillivirus
Poxviridae, genus Capripoxvirus
Herpesviridae, genus Varicellovirus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rinderpest virus belongs to Paramyxoviridae, genus Morbillivirus, closely related to canine distemper virus and PPR virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Picornaviridae, genus Aphthovirus: The classification of FMD virus, not rinderpest.
  • D. Herpesviridae, genus Varicellovirus: Not the classification of rinderpest virus; relevant instead to some herpesvirus diseases.
  • C. Poxviridae, genus Capripoxvirus: The classification of lumpy skin disease/sheep-goat pox virus, not rinderpest.

posts.post_content: The classic pathognomonic lesion of rinderpest is found in the:

_aimcq_options.text: Skin only
Reproductive tract only
Respiratory tract only
Alimentary tract — necrotic/erosive stomatitis with "zebra striping" of the large intestine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rinderpest shows classic necrotic/erosive stomatitis and "zebra striping" (linear haemorrhages) of the large intestinal mucosa, a hallmark alimentary tract lesion.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Respiratory tract only: Not the pathognomonic site; alimentary tract lesions are the defining feature of rinderpest.
  • A. Skin only: Not the pathognomonic site for rinderpest; skin lesions are more characteristic of pox diseases.
  • B. Reproductive tract only: Not the pathognomonic site for rinderpest.

posts.post_content: Rinderpest holds a unique distinction among animal diseases in that it was:

_aimcq_options.text: Only eradicated from a single country
Globally eradicated (declared by OIE/FAO in 2011)
Eradicated only in wildlife, not livestock
Never successfully controlled anywhere

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rinderpest was globally eradicated, officially declared by the OIE/FAO in 2011 — only the second disease ever eradicated globally (after smallpox in humans), through sustained vaccination campaigns.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Never successfully controlled anywhere: Incorrect — rinderpest was successfully controlled and ultimately eradicated worldwide.
  • A. Only eradicated from a single country: Understates the achievement — global eradication was declared, not just single-country elimination.
  • C. Eradicated only in wildlife, not livestock: Incorrect — eradication was achieved across both livestock and wildlife reservoirs globally.

posts.post_content: Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) primarily affects:

_aimcq_options.text: Only cattle
Only pigs
Sheep and goats (goats often more severely affected)
Only horses

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

PPR primarily affects sheep and goats, with goats often showing more severe disease than sheep; it is sometimes called "goat plague" or "pseudorinderpest of small ruminants".

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only cattle: Cattle can be subclinically infected but PPR's primary clinical impact is in small ruminants (sheep/goats), not cattle.
  • B. Only pigs: PPR does not primarily affect pigs; it is a small ruminant disease.
  • D. Only horses: PPR does not affect horses; it is a small ruminant disease.

posts.post_content: PPR clinically resembles rinderpest but in small ruminants, with characteristic signs including:

_aimcq_options.text: Painless nodular skin masses only
Only mild coughing with full recovery in all cases
Complete absence of any respiratory involvement
Fever, oculonasal discharge, necrotic stomatitis, and severe diarrhoea/pneumonia

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

PPR shows fever, oculonasal discharge, necrotic stomatitis, and severe diarrhoea often with pneumonia, closely mirroring rinderpest's presentation but in small ruminants.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Only mild coughing with full recovery in all cases: Understates the disease — PPR causes severe systemic illness with high mortality in susceptible populations, not merely mild self-limiting coughing.
  • A. Painless nodular skin masses only: Not the characteristic PPR presentation; this description is more consistent with pox-type skin diseases.
  • C. Complete absence of any respiratory involvement: Incorrect — pneumonia is a recognised and important component of PPR's clinical picture.

posts.post_content: Canine distemper virus (CDV) belongs to the same genus as rinderpest and PPR viruses, namely:

_aimcq_options.text: Pestivirus
Lentivirus
Morbillivirus
Orbivirus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CDV belongs to genus Morbillivirus, the same genus as rinderpest and PPR viruses, reflecting their shared systemic, immunosuppressive, and often neurotropic disease pattern.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Lentivirus: The genus for slow viral diseases like CAE and Visna-Maedi, not CDV.
  • A. Pestivirus: The genus for BVD-MD virus, not CDV.
  • D. Orbivirus: The genus for bluetongue/AHS viruses, not CDV.

posts.post_content: Canine distemper encephalitis is classically associated with which histopathological finding?

_aimcq_options.text: Intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in neurons/glial cells
Negri bodies exclusively
LCL bodies
Bollinger bodies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CDV encephalitis shows classic intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in neurons and glial cells, along with demyelination.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Negri bodies exclusively: Negri bodies are specific to rabies, not canine distemper, though both can affect the CNS.
  • D. Bollinger bodies: A fowl pox finding, not canine distemper.
  • C. LCL bodies: A chlamydial disease finding, not canine distemper.

posts.post_content: "Hard pad disease" in canine distemper refers to:

_aimcq_options.text: Hyperkeratosis of the footpads and nose
A specific vaccine reaction only
A skin tumour of the paw
Joint calcification

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Hard pad disease" refers to hyperkeratosis of the footpads and nose, a chronic dermatological manifestation of canine distemper virus infection.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. A skin tumour of the paw: Not the correct description; hyperkeratosis (thickening), not neoplasia, is the described change.
  • D. Joint calcification: Not the described feature of "hard pad disease".
  • B. A specific vaccine reaction only: Incorrect — this describes a natural infection manifestation, not a vaccine-specific reaction.

posts.post_content: Malignant catarrhal fever (MCF) in cattle occurs in two epidemiologically distinct forms associated with which reservoir hosts respectively?

_aimcq_options.text: Only a poultry-associated form
Wildebeest-associated and sheep-associated forms
Only a pig-associated form
Only a horse-associated form

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

MCF occurs as wildebeest-associated (Africa, via alcelaphine herpesvirus 1) and sheep-associated (worldwide, via ovine herpesvirus 2) forms, both causing severe disease in cattle as dead-end hosts.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only a pig-associated form: Not a recognised reservoir host association for MCF.
  • D. Only a horse-associated form: Not a recognised reservoir host association for MCF.
  • A. Only a poultry-associated form: Not a recognised reservoir host association for MCF.

posts.post_content: Cattle affected by MCF are considered "dead-end hosts" because they:

_aimcq_options.text: Develop severe/fatal disease but do not transmit virus to other cattle
Are the natural reservoir maintaining the virus
Transmit the virus efficiently to other cattle
Are completely immune and never show disease

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Cattle are "dead-end hosts" because they develop severe/fatal disease but do not transmit the virus onward to other cattle — the virus's natural reservoir is wildebeest or sheep, not cattle-to-cattle spread.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Are completely immune and never show disease: Incorrect — MCF is characteristically severe/fatal in affected cattle, not asymptomatic.
  • C. Transmit the virus efficiently to other cattle: Incorrect — this is precisely why cattle are called "dead-end" hosts; they do NOT efficiently transmit the virus onward.
  • B. Are the natural reservoir maintaining the virus: Incorrect — wildebeest/sheep are the natural reservoirs, not cattle.

posts.post_content: Persistently infected (PI) BVD virus calves arise from:

_aimcq_options.text: Vaccination at birth
Bacterial co-infection at any age
In utero infection with non-cytopathic BVDV before immunocompetence develops
Infection only after 6 months of age

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

PI calves arise from in utero infection with non-cytopathic BVDV before the fetal immune system becomes immunocompetent (roughly before day 125 of gestation), leading to immunotolerance and lifelong viral shedding.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Vaccination at birth: Not the mechanism of natural PI calf generation; PI status arises from specific-timing in utero infection, not vaccination.
  • D. Infection only after 6 months of age: Incorrect — PI status requires fetal infection during a specific early gestational window, not postnatal infection.
  • B. Bacterial co-infection at any age: Not the mechanism; PI status is specifically a consequence of the timing of viral (not bacterial) infection in utero.

posts.post_content: Fatal mucosal disease in BVD-MD occurs when a PI animal is superinfected with:

_aimcq_options.text: Any unrelated bacterial pathogen
A cytopathic biotype of BVDV, antigenically similar to its persisting non-cytopathic strain
Only bovine herpesvirus
Only Salmonella species

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Fatal mucosal disease occurs when a PI animal, immunotolerant to its own non-cytopathic BVDV strain, is superinfected with a cytopathic biotype antigenically similar to the persisting strain — the immune system cannot mount an effective response, leading to severe/fatal disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Any unrelated bacterial pathogen: Not the mechanism of mucosal disease, which is specifically a viral (cytopathic BVDV superinfection) phenomenon.
  • C. Only bovine herpesvirus: Not the mechanism of mucosal disease; a cytopathic BVDV strain, not herpesvirus, is required.
  • D. Only Salmonella species: Not the mechanism of mucosal disease, which is a specific BVDV biotype phenomenon.

posts.post_content: Infectious Bovine Rhinotracheitis (IBR) is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Bovine viral diarrhoea virus
Bovine herpesvirus 1 (BHV-1)
Bovine herpesvirus 4
Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

IBR is caused by Bovine herpesvirus 1 (BHV-1), which can also cause infectious pustular vulvovaginitis/balanoposthitis (IPV/IPB) as reproductive tract manifestations of the same virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Bovine herpesvirus 4: Not the causative agent of IBR; a different bovine herpesvirus type.
  • A. Bovine viral diarrhoea virus: The BVD-MD causative pestivirus, not the IBR causative herpesvirus.
  • D. Alcelaphine herpesvirus 1: The wildebeest-associated MCF virus, not the IBR causative agent.

posts.post_content: Like other alphaherpesviruses, BHV-1 (IBR virus) establishes latency primarily in the:

_aimcq_options.text: Bursa of Fabricius
Adrenal cortex
Trigeminal ganglion
Bone marrow

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

BHV-1 establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglion, similar to other alphaherpesviruses (e.g. ILTV in poultry), allowing recrudescence and shedding during stress.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bursa of Fabricius: An avian lymphoid organ relevant to IBDV, not a mammalian herpesvirus latency site.
  • D. Bone marrow: Not the described latency site for BHV-1.
  • B. Adrenal cortex: Not the described latency site for BHV-1.

posts.post_content: A classic pathological finding in cattle with MCF is:

_aimcq_options.text: Pericardial effusion resembling litchi fruit
Copper-bronze liver
Bursal atrophy
Fibrinoid necrotising vasculitis affecting multiple organs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

MCF is characterized by fibrinoid necrotising vasculitis affecting multiple organs, along with erosive/ulcerative lesions of the alimentary and respiratory mucosa and lymphoid proliferation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Bursal atrophy: An avian IBD-related lesion, not an MCF finding.
  • B. Copper-bronze liver: An avian fowl typhoid finding, not an MCF finding.
  • A. Pericardial effusion resembling litchi fruit: An avian hydropericardium syndrome finding, not an MCF finding.

posts.post_content: Bluetongue virus is transmitted by:

_aimcq_options.text: Ticks exclusively
Mosquitoes exclusively
Culicoides biting midges
Direct contact only, with no vector

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Bluetongue virus is transmitted by Culicoides biting midges, an essential insect vector for this orbivirus, explaining its seasonal and geographic distribution pattern.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Mosquitoes exclusively: Not the vector for bluetongue; Culicoides midges are specifically responsible.
  • A. Ticks exclusively: Not the vector for bluetongue virus transmission.
  • D. Direct contact only, with no vector: Incorrect — bluetongue is fundamentally a vector-borne (Culicoides-transmitted) disease, not a direct-contact disease.

posts.post_content: Among domestic ruminants, bluetongue clinical disease is generally most severe in:

_aimcq_options.text: Cattle
All species equally
Sheep
Goats

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Clinical bluetongue disease is generally most severe in sheep, while cattle and goats often show subclinical infection but can serve as reservoirs.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Cattle: Cattle typically show milder or subclinical disease compared to sheep, despite being an important reservoir host.
  • D. Goats: Goats also typically show milder disease compared to sheep.
  • B. All species equally: Incorrect — a clear species susceptibility difference exists, with sheep most severely affected.

posts.post_content: The name "bluetongue" derives from which classic clinical finding?

_aimcq_options.text: Blue-coloured wool
Blue eye colour change
Blue discolouration of the hooves only
Cyanosis of the tongue from vascular damage/hypoxia

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Bluetongue" derives from the cyanotic (blue) discolouration of the tongue resulting from vascular damage and hypoxia, though this specific sign is not seen in every case.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Blue-coloured wool: Not the source of the disease's name; the tongue cyanosis is specifically referenced.
  • C. Blue discolouration of the hooves only: Coronitis/hoof lesions occur in bluetongue, but the disease name specifically references the tongue, not the hooves.
  • B. Blue eye colour change: Not the source of the disease's name.

posts.post_content: African Horse Sickness (AHS), like bluetongue, is transmitted by the same vector genus:

_aimcq_options.text: Ticks only
Fleas only
Culicoides midges
Mosquitoes only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

AHS, another orbivirus disease, is also transmitted by Culicoides midges, similar to bluetongue virus, reflecting their shared genus (Orbivirus) and vector ecology.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Mosquitoes only: Not the vector for AHS; Culicoides midges are responsible.
  • A. Ticks only: Not the vector for AHS.
  • B. Fleas only: Not the vector for AHS.

posts.post_content: The peracute (pulmonary) form of AHS is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Skin nodules only
Painless joint swelling only
Chronic wasting over months with no respiratory signs
Severe respiratory distress with pulmonary oedema, rapid death

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The peracute (pulmonary) form shows severe respiratory distress with pulmonary oedema, causing rapid death — the most acute and highly fatal form of AHS.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Chronic wasting over months with no respiratory signs: This describes a chronic disease pattern, the opposite of the peracute pulmonary form's rapid respiratory-driven death.
  • A. Skin nodules only: Not the described pulmonary form presentation; skin nodules are more characteristic of pox diseases.
  • B. Painless joint swelling only: Not the described pulmonary form presentation.

posts.post_content: The subacute (cardiac) form of AHS is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Only skin lesions
Only diarrhoea
Only mild coughing with full recovery
Oedema of the head/neck/supraorbital fossa and cardiac failure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The subacute (cardiac) form shows oedema of the head, neck and supraorbital fossa along with cardiac failure, a distinct clinical pattern from the pulmonary form.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only mild coughing with full recovery: Understates the severity — the cardiac form is a serious, potentially fatal presentation, not a mild self-limiting condition.
  • A. Only skin lesions: Not the described cardiac form presentation; oedema and cardiac signs are specifically characteristic.
  • B. Only diarrhoea: Not the described cardiac form presentation.

posts.post_content: Both bluetongue virus and AHS virus belong to which viral family?

_aimcq_options.text: Reoviridae
Herpesviridae
Rhabdoviridae
Picornaviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Both belong to Reoviridae (genus Orbivirus), double-stranded RNA viruses with a segmented genome, transmitted by Culicoides midges.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Rhabdoviridae: The family for vesicular stomatitis and rabies viruses, not orbiviruses.
  • D. Picornaviridae: The family for FMD virus, not orbiviruses.
  • B. Herpesviridae: The family for herpesvirus diseases like IBR/MCF, not orbiviruses.

posts.post_content: Equine Infectious Anaemia (EIA) virus belongs to which genus?

_aimcq_options.text: Morbillivirus
Lentivirus
Orbivirus
Pestivirus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

EIA virus is a Lentivirus (family Retroviridae), producing a chronic, cyclical, immune-mediated disease with lifelong infection ("swamp fever").

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Morbillivirus: The genus for rinderpest/PPR/CDV, not EIA virus.
  • C. Orbivirus: The genus for bluetongue/AHS viruses, not EIA virus.
  • D. Pestivirus: The genus for BVD-MD virus, not EIA virus.

posts.post_content: EIA virus is primarily transmitted by:

_aimcq_options.text: Biting flies (mechanical transmission) and blood-contaminated equipment
Ingestion of contaminated feed only
Vertical transmission only
Airborne aerosol only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

EIA is primarily transmitted by biting flies (mechanical transmission of infected blood) and blood-contaminated equipment (needles, surgical instruments), given the virus's persistence in circulating blood cells.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Airborne aerosol only: Not the primary transmission route for EIA, which is blood-borne.
  • B. Ingestion of contaminated feed only: Not the primary transmission route for EIA.
  • C. Vertical transmission only: While vertical transmission can occur, it is not the primary/exclusive route; blood-borne mechanical transmission is emphasised.

posts.post_content: The standard confirmatory serological test for EIA is:

_aimcq_options.text: Tuberculin test
Coombs test
Dark-field microscopy
Coggins test (agar gel immunodiffusion)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The Coggins test (agar gel immunodiffusion) is the classic standard confirmatory test for EIA, required for interstate/international horse movement in many countries.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Tuberculin test: Used for tuberculosis diagnosis, not EIA.
  • B. Coombs test: Used for immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia diagnosis generally, not the standard EIA-specific test.
  • C. Dark-field microscopy: Used for spirochaete diagnosis, not EIA.

posts.post_content: Equine influenza virus belongs to which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Togaviridae
Rhabdoviridae
Orthomyxoviridae
Paramyxoviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Equine influenza virus belongs to Orthomyxoviridae, the same family as avian and human influenza viruses, causing acute respiratory disease with high morbidity but low mortality.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Paramyxoviridae: The family for morbilliviruses, not equine influenza.
  • B. Rhabdoviridae: The family for rabies/vesicular stomatitis viruses, not equine influenza.
  • A. Togaviridae: The family for equine encephalomyelitis viruses (EEE/WEE/VEE), not equine influenza.

posts.post_content: Equine Viral Arteritis (EVA) is caused by a virus of which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Picornaviridae
Arteriviridae
Orthomyxoviridae
Herpesviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

EVA is caused by a virus of family Arteriviridae, causing vasculitis, abortion, and (in stallions) a carrier state via persistent infection of the reproductive tract.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Herpesviridae: The family for equine rhinopneumonitis virus (EHV), not EVA virus.
  • C. Orthomyxoviridae: The family for equine influenza virus, not EVA virus.
  • A. Picornaviridae: The family for FMD virus, not EVA virus.

posts.post_content: Equine rhinopneumonitis is caused by which viruses, associated with respiratory disease and abortion?

_aimcq_options.text: Equine arteritis virus
Equine encephalomyelitis virus
Equine influenza virus
Equine herpesvirus 1 and 4 (EHV-1, EHV-4)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Equine rhinopneumonitis is caused by Equine herpesvirus 1 and 4 (EHV-1, EHV-4), with EHV-1 particularly associated with abortion and neurological disease, and EHV-4 primarily with respiratory disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Equine influenza virus: Causes a distinct acute respiratory disease, not the herpesvirus-caused rhinopneumonitis.
  • A. Equine arteritis virus: Causes EVA, a distinct arterivirus disease, not rhinopneumonitis.
  • B. Equine encephalomyelitis virus: Causes a distinct neurological (togavirus) disease, not rhinopneumonitis.

posts.post_content: Eastern, Western, and Venezuelan equine encephalomyelitis viruses (togaviruses) are transmitted by:

_aimcq_options.text: Culicoides midges
Mosquitoes
Direct contact only

posts.post_content: Caprine Arthritis Encephalitis (CAE) virus is classified as a:

_aimcq_options.text: Morbillivirus (Paramyxoviridae)
Lentivirus (Retroviridae)
Orbivirus (Reoviridae)
Pestivirus (Flaviviridae)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CAE virus is a Lentivirus within Retroviridae, related to Visna-Maedi virus of sheep, causing a slow, progressive, multisystemic disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Morbillivirus (Paramyxoviridae): Not the classification of CAE virus; this describes rinderpest/PPR/CDV instead.
  • C. Orbivirus (Reoviridae): Not the classification of CAE virus; this describes bluetongue/AHS viruses.
  • D. Pestivirus (Flaviviridae): Not the classification of CAE virus; this describes BVD-MD virus.

posts.post_content: CAE presents in two main clinical forms depending on age:

_aimcq_options.text: Only skin lesions at any age
Only reproductive failure at any age
Only respiratory disease at any age
Encephalitis in young kids, arthritis in adult goats

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

CAE presents as encephalitis in young kids (typically 2-4 months) and chronic arthritis in adult goats, reflecting age-related tissue tropism differences of the lentivirus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only respiratory disease at any age: Not the described dual clinical pattern; encephalitis (young) and arthritis (adult) are specifically named.
  • B. Only reproductive failure at any age: Not the described dual clinical pattern for CAE.

posts.post_content: Visna-Maedi virus in sheep causes two distinct disease forms named for their target organ:

_aimcq_options.text: Only a reproductive form
Visna (neurological/CNS) and Maedi (progressive pneumonia)
Only a single gastrointestinal form
Only a skin form

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The virus causes "Visna" (progressive neurological/demyelinating CNS disease) and "Maedi" (progressive interstitial pneumonia), both slow, chronic, ultimately fatal lentiviral diseases of sheep.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only a single gastrointestinal form: Not accurate — the virus specifically causes two named forms (neurological and respiratory), not a GI form.
  • D. Only a skin form: Not accurate — the two named forms are neurological and respiratory, not dermatological.
  • A. Only a reproductive form: Not accurate — the two named forms are neurological and respiratory, not reproductive.

posts.post_content: Jaagsiekte (Ovine Pulmonary Adenocarcinoma, OPA) is caused by a virus of which type, distinct from Visna-Maedi?

_aimcq_options.text: A lentivirus identical to Visna-Maedi virus
A betaretrovirus (Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus, JSRV)
A poxvirus
A herpesvirus

Correct Answer Explanation

Jaagsiekte is caused by Jaagsiekte sheep retrovirus (JSRV), a betaretrovirus distinct from the lentivirus causing Visna-Maedi, though both cause chronic pulmonary disease in sheep.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. A lentivirus identical to Visna-Maedi virus: Incorrect — JSRV is a distinct betaretrovirus, not the same lentivirus causing Visna-Maedi.
  • D. A herpesvirus: Not the classification of JSRV.

posts.post_content: Jaagsiekte is unique among these lentivirus/retrovirus small ruminant diseases in that it causes:

_aimcq_options.text: Only inflammatory (non-neoplastic) pneumonia
Only skin nodules
Only joint disease
A transmissible lung adenocarcinoma (neoplastic transformation of alveolar/bronchiolar epithelium)

Jaagsiekte is unique in causing a transmissible lung adenocarcinoma — actual neoplastic transformation of alveolar/bronchiolar epithelial cells — distinct from the purely inflammatory pneumonia of Maedi.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only inflammatory (non-neoplastic) pneumonia: This describes Maedi, not Jaagsiekte, which specifically causes a neoplastic (adenocarcinoma) lung disease.
  • C. Only joint disease: Not the described disease pattern for Jaagsiekte, which is specifically pulmonary/neoplastic.
  • B. Only skin nodules: Not the described disease pattern for Jaagsiekte.

posts.post_content: CAE, Visna-Maedi, and similar lentivirus diseases share which common epidemiological feature?

_aimcq_options.text: Rapid onset and resolution within days
No lifelong persistence of the virus
Long incubation periods with slow, progressive, ultimately fatal disease course
Complete self-cure without intervention

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

These lentivirus diseases share long incubation periods with a slow, progressive, ultimately fatal disease course — hence the term "lentivirus" (Latin "lentus" = slow).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Rapid onset and resolution within days: The opposite of lentiviral disease behaviour, which is characteristically slow and chronic, not rapid and self-resolving.
  • D. Complete self-cure without intervention: Incorrect — these are progressive, ultimately fatal diseases, not self-curing conditions.
  • B. No lifelong persistence of the virus: Incorrect — lifelong viral persistence is a hallmark feature of lentivirus infections.

posts.post_content: The primary route of CAE virus transmission to kids is:

Insect vector bite
Airborne only, unrelated to nursing
Direct venereal transmission only

The primary transmission route is ingestion of infected colostrum/milk from the dam, making colostrum management (heat treatment, colostrum replacers) a key control strategy.

  • C. Airborne only, unrelated to nursing: Not the primary described transmission route for CAE; colostrum/milk ingestion is specifically emphasised.
  • B. Insect vector bite: Not the transmission route for CAE virus, unlike vector-borne diseases such as bluetongue.
  • D. Direct venereal transmission only: Not the primary described transmission route; colostrum/milk-borne spread to kids is the key route.

posts.post_content: Classical Swine Fever (Hog Cholera) virus is classified as a:

Lentivirus
Morbillivirus
Pestivirus (Flaviviridae), related to BVD-MD virus

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Morbillivirus: Not the classification of classical swine fever virus; this describes rinderpest/PPR/CDV.
  • A. Orbivirus: Not the classification of classical swine fever virus; this describes bluetongue/AHS.

posts.post_content: The classic gross lesion of classical swine fever involves:

_aimcq_options.text: Bursal atrophy only
"Turkey-egg" (button) haemorrhagic infarcts of the spleen and petechiae throughout organs
Cerebellar oedema only
Copper-bronze liver only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Classical swine fever shows classic "turkey-egg" (button) haemorrhagic splenic infarcts and widespread petechial haemorrhages throughout multiple organs, reflecting the severe vasculitis and thrombocytopenia caused by the virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Copper-bronze liver only: An avian fowl typhoid finding, not the classic swine fever lesion.
  • A. Bursal atrophy only: An avian IBD-related finding, not a swine fever lesion.
  • C. Cerebellar oedema only: An avian vitamin E deficiency finding, not the classic swine fever lesion.

posts.post_content: Swine influenza virus belongs to which viral family, shared with human and avian influenza?

_aimcq_options.text: Picornaviridae
Orthomyxoviridae
Coronaviridae
Paramyxoviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:

Swine influenza virus belongs to Orthomyxoviridae, the same family shared with human and avian influenza viruses, with pigs serving as an important "mixing vessel" for reassortment between avian/human/swine strains.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Paramyxoviridae: Not the family for influenza viruses; this describes morbilliviruses instead.
  • C. Coronaviridae: Not the family for influenza viruses; this describes coronaviruses like TGE/PED.
