posts.post_content: Aujeszky's disease (pseudorabies) is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Swine influenza virus
Classical swine fever virus
Porcine parvovirus
Suid herpesvirus 1

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Aujeszky's disease is caused by Suid herpesvirus 1, an alphaherpesvirus causing severe neurological disease particularly in young pigs, and often fatal disease in other species (dogs, cats, cattle) that become dead-end hosts.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Classical swine fever virus: The pestivirus causing classical swine fever, a distinct disease from Aujeszky's.
  • A. Swine influenza virus: The orthomyxovirus causing swine influenza, a distinct respiratory disease.
  • C. Porcine parvovirus: Causes reproductive failure (SMEDI) in pigs, not Aujeszky's disease.

posts.post_content: Aujeszky's disease is also commonly known as:

_aimcq_options.text: Pseudorabies
Blue ear disease
Mulberry heart disease
Blackleg

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Aujeszky's disease is also commonly known as pseudorabies, reflecting its severe pruritic/neurological presentation that can resemble rabies, particularly the characteristic intense itching ("mad itch") seen in some species.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Blackleg: The common name for Clostridium chauvoei myonecrosis in cattle, an entirely different (bacterial) disease.
  • B. Blue ear disease: A common name associated with porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS), not Aujeszky's disease.
  • C. Mulberry heart disease: A vitamin E/selenium deficiency-related cardiac condition in pigs, not Aujeszky's disease.

posts.post_content: Compared to pigs (the natural reservoir), other species (dogs, cats, cattle) infected with Aujeszky's virus typically show:

_aimcq_options.text: Rapidly fatal disease with intense pruritus, as dead-end hosts
No disease of any kind
Chronic, slowly progressive disease over years
Mild, self-limiting disease with full recovery

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Non-porcine species typically show rapidly fatal disease with intense pruritus, acting as dead-end hosts that do not efficiently transmit the virus further, unlike the natural pig reservoir where disease severity varies more by age.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Mild, self-limiting disease with full recovery: Incorrect — the disease is typically rapidly fatal in these dead-end host species, not mild/self-limiting.
  • B. No disease of any kind: Incorrect — these species characteristically develop severe, often fatal disease upon infection.
  • C. Chronic, slowly progressive disease over years: Incorrect — the disease course in these dead-end hosts is typically rapid and fatal, not chronic over years.

posts.post_content: Congenital infection with classical swine fever virus (analogous to BVD-MD PI calves) can result in:

_aimcq_options.text: Persistently infected, immunotolerant piglets shedding virus
No possibility of in utero infection
Complete fetal immunity with no consequence
Piglets born with full protective antibodies only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Congenital infection, similar to the BVD-MD mechanism, can produce persistently infected, immunotolerant piglets that continuously shed virus, posing an ongoing transmission risk within the herd.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Complete fetal immunity with no consequence: Incorrect — congenital infection specifically leads to immunotolerance and persistent shedding, not protective immunity with no consequence.
  • D. Piglets born with full protective antibodies only: Incorrect — the immunotolerant mechanism means these piglets fail to mount an effective antibody response, not that they're born fully protected.
  • B. No possibility of in utero infection: Incorrect — in utero infection and the resulting persistent infection state is a well-recognised phenomenon for this pestivirus, paralleling BVD-MD.

posts.post_content: Rabies virus belongs to which family?

_aimcq_options.text: Rhabdoviridae
Paramyxoviridae
Reoviridae
Orthomyxoviridae

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rabies virus belongs to Rhabdoviridae (genus Lyssavirus), a bullet-shaped, enveloped RNA virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Paramyxoviridae: The family for morbilliviruses, not rabies virus.
  • D. Orthomyxoviridae: The family for influenza viruses, not rabies virus.
  • C. Reoviridae: The family for orbiviruses, not rabies virus.

posts.post_content: The pathognomonic histopathological finding in rabies is:

_aimcq_options.text: Bollinger bodies
Negri bodies — intracytoplasmic inclusions in neurons, especially hippocampal pyramidal cells
Reed-Sternberg-like cells
LCL bodies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The pathognomonic finding is Negri bodies — eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in neurons, especially in hippocampal pyramidal cells and Purkinje cells, representing viral nucleocapsid aggregates.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Bollinger bodies: A fowl pox finding, not rabies.
  • D. LCL bodies: A chlamydial disease finding, not rabies.
  • C. Reed-Sternberg-like cells: Not a rabies-related finding; associated with lymphoma-type conditions.

posts.post_content: Rabies virus is most commonly transmitted via:

_aimcq_options.text: Airborne aerosol transmission in all settings
Insect vector bite
Ingestion of contaminated feed
Bite wound introducing infected saliva

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rabies is most commonly transmitted via a bite wound introducing infected saliva from a rabid animal, with the virus then travelling retrograde along peripheral nerves to the CNS.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Airborne aerosol transmission in all settings: Not the typical/common transmission route; while rare aerosol transmission has been documented in specific settings (e.g. bat caves), bite-wound transmission is the standard route.
  • C. Ingestion of contaminated feed: Not the typical transmission route for rabies virus.
  • B. Insect vector bite: Not the transmission route for rabies, which is a direct bite-wound (mammalian) disease, unlike vector-borne diseases such as bluetongue.

posts.post_content: The "dumb" (paralytic) form of rabies is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Extreme aggression and biting behaviour
Complete absence of any neurological signs
Progressive paralysis with minimal aggression
Only gastrointestinal signs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The "dumb" (paralytic) form is characterized by progressive paralysis with minimal aggression, in contrast to the "furious" form, which shows marked aggression/hyperexcitability.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Extreme aggression and biting behaviour: This describes the "furious" form, not the "dumb" (paralytic) form, which is characterized by the opposite pattern of paralysis rather than aggression.
  • B. Complete absence of any neurological signs: Incorrect — rabies is fundamentally a neurological disease; the "dumb" form still shows neurological signs (paralysis), just without the aggressive component.
  • D. Only gastrointestinal signs: Not the described feature of the "dumb" form, which is specifically characterized by paralysis.

posts.post_content: The incubation period of rabies is notably variable and depends significantly on:

_aimcq_options.text: The site/severity of the bite wound relative to the CNS
The animal's diet exclusively
The colour of the animal's fur
The time of year exclusively

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Incubation period variability depends significantly on the site/severity of the bite wound relative to the CNS — bites closer to the head/face generally have shorter incubation periods than bites on distal extremities, since the virus must travel along peripheral nerves to reach the brain.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. The colour of the animal's fur: Not a factor influencing rabies incubation period.
  • D. The time of year exclusively: Not the primary described factor; wound site/severity relative to the CNS is specifically emphasised.
  • B. The animal's diet exclusively: Not a factor influencing rabies incubation period.

posts.post_content: The gold-standard postmortem diagnostic test for rabies is:

_aimcq_options.text: Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test on brain tissue
Blood culture
Skin biopsy of the tail
Faecal examination

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The gold-standard postmortem test is the direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) test on brain tissue (typically hippocampus, cerebellum, brainstem), providing rapid and highly sensitive/specific results.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Blood culture: Not the diagnostic method for rabies, which is not typically detectable via blood culture.
  • D. Faecal examination: Not relevant to rabies diagnosis, which is a CNS-focused viral disease.
  • C. Skin biopsy of the tail: Not the gold-standard postmortem test; while antemortem nuchal skin biopsy has some diagnostic use in humans, brain tissue DFA is the postmortem gold standard in animals.

posts.post_content: Rabies reservoir species vary by geographic region; in much of the developing world, the primary reservoir/vector is:

_aimcq_options.text: Bats exclusively
Skunks exclusively
Raccoons exclusively
Domestic dogs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

In much of the developing world, domestic dogs remain the primary reservoir/vector for rabies transmission to humans and other animals, making dog vaccination programmes central to control efforts in these regions.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Raccoons exclusively: A significant reservoir species in certain regions (e.g. parts of North America), but not the primary global reservoir described for much of the developing world.
  • A. Bats exclusively: An important reservoir in some contexts, but not the primary reservoir specifically described for much of the developing world, where dogs dominate.
  • B. Skunks exclusively: A regional reservoir species in some areas, but not the primary global reservoir described here.

posts.post_content: Infectious Canine Hepatitis (ICH) is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Canine parvovirus
Feline panleucopenia virus
Canine adenovirus 1 (CAV-1)
Canine distemper virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

ICH is caused by Canine adenovirus 1 (CAV-1), a DNA virus causing acute hepatic necrosis, and classically associated with "blue eye" (corneal oedema) in recovering dogs.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Canine parvovirus: Causes canine parvoviral enteritis/myocarditis, a distinct disease from ICH.
  • D. Canine distemper virus: A morbillivirus causing a distinct systemic/neurological disease, not ICH.
  • B. Feline panleucopenia virus: The feline-specific parvovirus, not the canine ICH agent.

posts.post_content: "Blue eye" in dogs recovering from ICH results from:

_aimcq_options.text: Cataract formation from lens protein denaturation
Conjunctival haemorrhage
Corneal oedema from an immune-complex reaction
Direct viral destruction of the retina

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Blue eye" results from corneal oedema caused by an immune-complex (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction in the anterior uvea/cornea, occurring in some dogs during recovery from ICH.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Direct viral destruction of the retina: Not the mechanism of "blue eye"; the finding is corneal, immune-mediated, not direct retinal viral destruction.
  • A. Cataract formation from lens protein denaturation: Not the mechanism of "blue eye"; this describes a different ocular pathology (cataract), while "blue eye" is corneal oedema.
  • B. Conjunctival haemorrhage: Not the described mechanism/appearance of "blue eye", which specifically involves corneal oedema.

posts.post_content: Canine parvovirus preferentially infects rapidly dividing cells, particularly in the:

_aimcq_options.text: Only mature, non-dividing neurons
Intestinal crypt epithelium and bone marrow/lymphoid tissue
Only fully keratinised skin
Only cartilage

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Canine parvovirus preferentially infects rapidly dividing cells in the intestinal crypt epithelium and bone marrow/lymphoid tissue, explaining the classic enteritis and leukopenia seen in affected dogs.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only mature, non-dividing neurons: Not the primary target; the virus specifically targets rapidly dividing cell populations, and mature neurons are largely non-dividing (though myocarditis in very young pups reflects a different tropism).
  • C. Only fully keratinised skin: Not the primary target of canine parvovirus, which is rapidly dividing intestinal/lymphoid/marrow cells.
  • D. Only cartilage: Not the primary target of canine parvovirus.

posts.post_content: Feline panleucopenia virus is closely related to (and can cross-infect with) which other parvovirus?

_aimcq_options.text: Bovine parvovirus
Human parvovirus B19
Canine parvovirus
Porcine parvovirus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Feline panleucopenia virus is closely related to canine parvovirus, reflecting their shared evolutionary origin, with canine parvovirus having emerged as a host-range variant capable of infecting dogs.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Porcine parvovirus: Not closely related in the way described between feline panleucopenia and canine parvovirus.
  • A. Bovine parvovirus: Not the specifically described closely related cross-infecting parvovirus in this context.
  • B. Human parvovirus B19: Not the specifically described closely related cross-infecting parvovirus in this context.

posts.post_content: In utero or very early postnatal infection with feline panleucopenia virus can cause which neurological defect in kittens?

_aimcq_options.text: Cerebellar hypoplasia
No neurological effects, only GI signs
Spinal bifida exclusively
Complete brain absence (anencephaly)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

In utero or very early postnatal infection can cause cerebellar hypoplasia, since the virus targets rapidly dividing cerebellar Purkinje cell precursors during this critical developmental window, producing lifelong ataxia in surviving kittens.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Complete brain absence (anencephaly): Overstates the described defect; the specific finding is cerebellar hypoplasia, not complete absence of the brain.
  • C. Spinal bifida exclusively: Not the described defect associated with feline panleucopenia congenital infection; cerebellar hypoplasia is specifically named.
  • B. No neurological effects, only GI signs: Incorrect — the congenital/perinatal form specifically causes a distinct neurological (cerebellar) defect, in contrast to the GI form seen in older cats.

posts.post_content: Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) arises from mutation of which more benign virus?

_aimcq_options.text: Feline calicivirus
Feline herpesvirus
Feline enteric coronavirus
Feline leukaemia virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

FIP arises from mutation of feline enteric coronavirus within an infected cat, converting a generally mild/asymptomatic enteric infection into a systemic, highly pathogenic disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Feline calicivirus: Causes a distinct upper respiratory/oral disease in cats, not the origin virus for FIP.
  • B. Feline herpesvirus: Causes feline viral rhinotracheitis, a distinct respiratory disease, not the origin virus for FIP.
  • D. Feline leukaemia virus: A distinct retrovirus causing immunosuppression/neoplasia, not the origin virus for FIP.

posts.post_content: FIP presents in two main forms based on the immune response, namely:

_aimcq_options.text: Effusive ("wet") and non-effusive ("dry") forms
Only a musculoskeletal form
Only a respiratory form
Only a dermatological form

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

FIP presents as effusive ("wet", with fluid accumulation in body cavities) and non-effusive ("dry", with pyogranulomatous lesions in organs) forms, reflecting the balance between humoral and cell-mediated immune responses to the mutated virus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only a respiratory form: Not the described dual classification for FIP, which is specifically effusive vs non-effusive.
  • D. Only a dermatological form: Not the described dual classification for FIP.
  • B. Only a musculoskeletal form: Not the described dual classification for FIP.

posts.post_content: Prions, the causative agents of scrapie/BSE, are unique among infectious agents in that they are:

_aimcq_options.text: Standard RNA viruses
Bacteria with a resistant spore form
Composed entirely of abnormal protein with no nucleic acid
Standard DNA viruses

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Prions are unique in being composed entirely of abnormal (misfolded) protein with no nucleic acid, propagating by inducing conformational change in normal host prion protein (PrP^C to PrP^Sc).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Standard DNA viruses: Incorrect — prions lack any nucleic acid genome, unlike conventional DNA viruses.
  • A. Standard RNA viruses: Incorrect — prions lack any nucleic acid genome, unlike conventional RNA viruses.
  • B. Bacteria with a resistant spore form: Incorrect — prions are not bacteria; they are solely composed of misfolded protein.

posts.post_content: Scrapie is a prion disease primarily affecting:

_aimcq_options.text: Sheep and goats
Only pigs
Only horses
Only cattle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Scrapie primarily affects sheep and goats, causing a progressive, fatal spongiform encephalopathy with pruritus ("scrapie" from the characteristic scraping/rubbing behaviour).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Only cattle: Not the primary scrapie host species; cattle are instead the primary host for BSE.
  • B. Only pigs: Not a natural host species for scrapie.
  • C. Only horses: Not a natural host species for scrapie.

posts.post_content: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) is thought to have originated in cattle largely through:

_aimcq_options.text: Airborne transmission from wild birds
Contaminated drinking water alone
Feeding of contaminated meat-and-bone meal derived from infected animals
Insect vector transmission

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

BSE is thought to have originated largely through feeding contaminated meat-and-bone meal derived from infected animals (initially theorised as scrapie-origin, later understood as a distinct cattle-adapted prion), amplifying and spreading via the rendering-feed cycle.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Airborne transmission from wild birds: Not the theorised route of BSE origin/spread; feed-borne transmission via rendered animal protein is specifically implicated.
  • D. Insect vector transmission: Not the theorised route of BSE origin/spread.
  • B. Contaminated drinking water alone: Not the primary theorised route of BSE origin/spread; feed-borne transmission is specifically implicated.

posts.post_content: BSE gained major public health significance due to its link with which human prion disease?

_aimcq_options.text: Alzheimer's disease
Multiple sclerosis
Parkinson's disease
Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

BSE gained major significance due to its link with variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD) in humans, believed to result from consumption of BSE-contaminated beef products, establishing BSE as a zoonotic prion disease.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Alzheimer's disease: A distinct neurodegenerative condition, not a prion disease linked to BSE.
  • C. Parkinson's disease: A distinct neurodegenerative condition, not a prion disease linked to BSE.
  • B. Multiple sclerosis: An autoimmune demyelinating condition, not a prion disease linked to BSE.

posts.post_content: The characteristic microscopic finding in prion diseases (spongiform encephalopathies) is:

_aimcq_options.text: Vacuolation (spongy change) of the neuropil, without inflammation
Granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis
Marked neutrophilic inflammation
Negri body inclusions

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The characteristic finding is vacuolation (spongy change) of the neuropil, giving the tissue a sponge-like microscopic appearance, notably without an inflammatory response — distinguishing prion diseases from typical infectious encephalitides.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Marked neutrophilic inflammation: Incorrect — the notable absence of inflammation is a key distinguishing feature of prion disease pathology.
  • D. Negri body inclusions: The characteristic finding for rabies, not prion diseases, which show spongiform vacuolation instead.
  • B. Granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis: A tuberculosis-type finding, not the non-inflammatory spongiform change characteristic of prion diseases.

posts.post_content: Prions are notable for being highly resistant to:

_aimcq_options.text: All forms of heat exposure of any duration/temperature
Standard sterilisation methods (routine autoclaving, formalin fixation, standard disinfectants)
Only UV light exposure
Only freezing

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Prions are highly resistant to standard sterilisation methods — routine autoclaving, formalin fixation, and standard disinfectants — requiring specialised protocols (extended high-temperature autoclaving, strong alkali/hypochlorite treatment) for effective inactivation.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. All forms of heat exposure of any duration/temperature: Overstates the resistance — prions CAN be inactivated by sufficiently extended, high-temperature specialised protocols, just not by routine/standard methods.
  • C. Only UV light exposure: Understates the resistance profile — prions resist a broad range of standard methods, not merely UV light specifically.
  • D. Only freezing: Understates the resistance profile — prions resist a broad range of standard sterilisation approaches, not merely freezing.

posts.post_content: Feline Spongiform Encephalopathy (FSE), reported in domestic and captive wild cats, is thought to be linked to:

_aimcq_options.text: Only insect-vector transmission
Exposure to BSE-contaminated feed/meat products
A completely unrelated, spontaneously arising feline-specific prion with no external source
Only a genetic mutation with no infectious component

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

FSE is thought to be linked to exposure to BSE-contaminated feed/meat products, representing cross-species prion transmission from cattle to cats, paralleling the BSE-vCJD link in humans.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. A completely unrelated, spontaneously arising feline-specific prion with no external source: Incorrect — the epidemiological pattern and timing strongly implicated dietary exposure to BSE-contaminated material, not a spontaneous unrelated origin.
  • A. Only insect-vector transmission: Not the implicated route for FSE; dietary/feed-borne exposure is specifically theorised.
  • D. Only a genetic mutation with no infectious component: Incorrect — the infectious (prion cross-species transmission) theory, not a purely genetic mechanism, is the recognised explanation for FSE's emergence.

posts.post_content: Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) of cattle is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Bovine papular stomatitis virus
Orf virus
Capripoxvirus (Neethling virus)
Cowpox virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

LSD is caused by a Capripoxvirus (Neethling virus), closely related to sheep pox and goat pox viruses, causing characteristic nodular skin lesions in cattle.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Orf virus: Causes contagious ecthyma (orf) in sheep/goats, a distinct parapoxvirus disease, not LSD.
  • A. Bovine papular stomatitis virus: A distinct parapoxvirus causing oral papules in cattle, not the causative agent of LSD.
  • D. Cowpox virus: A distinct orthopoxvirus, not the LSD causative agent (which is a capripoxvirus).

posts.post_content: Lumpy skin disease is believed to spread mainly via:

_aimcq_options.text: Only transovarian transmission
Airborne aerosol exclusively
Mechanical transmission by biting insects (flies, mosquitoes, ticks)
Only direct oral ingestion

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

LSD is believed to spread mainly via mechanical transmission by biting insects (flies, mosquitoes, ticks), explaining its seasonal pattern coinciding with insect activity.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Airborne aerosol exclusively: Not the primary/described transmission route for LSD; insect-borne mechanical transmission is emphasised instead.
  • D. Only direct oral ingestion: Not the primary described transmission route for LSD.
  • A. Only transovarian transmission: Not applicable to cattle (a non-egg-laying species) and not the described transmission route for LSD.

posts.post_content: Orf (contagious ecthyma) in sheep/goats is notable for being:

_aimcq_options.text: Only affecting internal organs, sparing the skin
Zoonotic, capable of causing skin lesions in humans handling infected animals
Never transmissible to humans under any circumstances
Fatal in nearly all affected animals

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Orf is notable for being zoonotic, capable of causing localized skin lesions in humans (particularly farmers, shearers, veterinarians) who handle infected animals.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Never transmissible to humans under any circumstances: Incorrect — orf is a well-recognised zoonosis affecting people in direct contact with infected animals.
  • A. Only affecting internal organs, sparing the skin: Incorrect — orf is fundamentally a skin (mucocutaneous, particularly around the mouth/lips) disease, not an internal organ disease.
  • D. Fatal in nearly all affected animals: Incorrect — orf is typically self-limiting in affected animals, not routinely fatal.

posts.post_content: The classic lesion distribution in orf (contagious ecthyma) affects primarily the:

_aimcq_options.text: Only the udder
Only the internal viscera
Only the hooves
Lips, muzzle, and oral mucosa

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Orf classically affects the lips, muzzle, and oral mucosa, producing proliferative scabby lesions that can interfere with nursing/feeding, particularly in young lambs/kids.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Only the udder: Not the classic/primary lesion site for orf, though udder lesions can occur secondarily (e.g. from nursing lambs); the mouth/lips is the classic site.
  • C. Only the hooves: Not the classic lesion site for orf.
  • B. Only the internal viscera: Incorrect — orf is a mucocutaneous (external) disease, not an internal visceral disease.

posts.post_content: Bovine papular stomatitis, caused by a parapoxvirus, is generally:

_aimcq_options.text: A disease with no known zoonotic potential whatsoever
A mild, self-limiting disease of the oral mucosa in young cattle
A highly fatal systemic disease
Exclusively a disease of adult cattle

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Bovine papular stomatitis is generally a mild, self-limiting disease affecting the oral mucosa, most commonly seen in young cattle, and is often an incidental finding.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. A highly fatal systemic disease: Incorrect — the disease is characteristically mild and self-limiting, not highly fatal/systemic.
  • D. Exclusively a disease of adult cattle: Incorrect — young cattle are specifically noted as most commonly affected, not exclusively adults.
  • A. A disease with no known zoonotic potential whatsoever: Not accurate — as a parapoxvirus related to orf and pseudocowpox, some zoonotic potential is recognised, though the disease is primarily notable for its mild bovine presentation.

posts.post_content: Poxviruses, including LSD virus, orf virus, and others in this family, are characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: No genome at all, being purely protein-based
Large, complex dsDNA genomes with cytoplasmic replication
Segmented dsRNA genomes
Small, simple ssRNA genomes with nuclear replication

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Poxviruses are characterized by large, complex dsDNA genomes with cytoplasmic replication — unusual among DNA viruses, most of which replicate in the nucleus.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Small, simple ssRNA genomes with nuclear replication: Incorrect — poxviruses have large dsDNA genomes with cytoplasmic (not nuclear) replication.
  • C. Segmented dsRNA genomes: This describes orbiviruses/reoviruses, not poxviruses.
  • A. No genome at all, being purely protein-based: This describes prions, not poxviruses, which have substantial dsDNA genomes.

posts.post_content: Classic pox lesions in susceptible animals typically progress through which sequence?

_aimcq_options.text: Directly from normal skin to scab with no intermediate stages
Macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → scab
Vesicle → macule → papule only
Scab formation immediately, with no preceding stages

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Classic pox lesions progress through the sequence macule → papule → vesicle → pustule → scab, reflecting the stages of local viral replication, inflammation, and eventual healing.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Directly from normal skin to scab with no intermediate stages: Incorrect — the characteristic staged progression through multiple lesion types is a defining feature of pox disease presentation.
  • C. Vesicle → macule → papule only: Incorrect order — the correct sequence begins with macule/papule and progresses to vesicle/pustule/scab, not this reversed/incomplete order.
  • D. Scab formation immediately, with no preceding stages: Incorrect — scab formation is the final stage, following the earlier macule/papule/vesicle/pustule progression, not an immediate first step.

posts.post_content: Rotavirus enteritis in neonatal animals results from infection and destruction of:

_aimcq_options.text: Only the liver
Mature villous enterocytes, causing malabsorptive diarrhoea
Only crypt stem cells, sparing villous tips
Only the large intestine, sparing the small intestine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rotavirus infects and destroys mature villous enterocytes (particularly at the villous tips), causing villous atrophy and malabsorptive diarrhoea in neonates.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only crypt stem cells, sparing villous tips: Incorrect — rotavirus specifically targets the mature villous tip enterocytes, not the crypt stem cells (which actually help drive subsequent regeneration).
  • D. Only the large intestine, sparing the small intestine: Incorrect — rotavirus primarily affects the small intestine, where nutrient-absorbing villous enterocytes are concentrated.
  • A. Only the liver: Incorrect — rotavirus is an enteric (intestinal) pathogen, not a hepatotropic virus.

posts.post_title: Coronavirus Enteric Disease Comparison to Rotavirus
posts.post_content: Compared to rotavirus, enteric coronavirus infection in neonates often causes:

_aimcq_options.text: No diarrhoea whatsoever
Only respiratory signs, no GI involvement
Identical, indistinguishable disease severity in all cases
More severe disease, since it can also infect crypt cells, impairing regenerative capacity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Enteric coronavirus often causes more severe disease than rotavirus, since it can also infect crypt cells (not just villous tips), impairing the intestine's regenerative capacity and prolonging recovery.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Identical, indistinguishable disease severity in all cases: Incorrect — a recognised difference in severity exists, with coronavirus often causing more severe disease due to its broader (crypt plus villous) cell tropism.
  • A. No diarrhoea whatsoever: Incorrect — enteric coronavirus is specifically a cause of neonatal diarrhoea, similar in presentation (though often more severe) to rotavirus.
  • B. Only respiratory signs, no GI involvement: Incorrect — in this enteric context, GI (diarrhoeal) disease is the primary presentation, not respiratory disease.

posts.post_content: Neonatal rotavirus/coronavirus enteritis is most severe in animals of what age?

_aimcq_options.text: Only immediately before puberty
Very young (first days to weeks of life)
Only in adults over 5 years
Age has no bearing on severity

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Disease is most severe in very young animals (first days to weeks of life), when the intestinal mucosa is most vulnerable and dehydration from diarrhoea poses the greatest life-threatening risk.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Only in adults over 5 years: Incorrect — these are specifically neonatal diseases, with young age (not adulthood) being the key susceptibility factor.
  • A. Only immediately before puberty: Not the described age group; very young neonates are specifically emphasised.
  • D. Age has no bearing on severity: Incorrect — age is a critical determinant of disease severity in these neonatal enteric infections.

posts.post_content: Death from neonatal rotavirus/coronavirus enteritis most commonly results from:

_aimcq_options.text: Severe dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base imbalance
Liver failure exclusively
Direct viral destruction of the heart
Bone marrow failure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Death most commonly results from severe dehydration and electrolyte/acid-base imbalance secondary to the profuse diarrhoea and malabsorption, making fluid/electrolyte support a critical treatment component.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Direct viral destruction of the heart: Not the primary described mortality mechanism for these enteric viruses, which target intestinal epithelium, not cardiac tissue.
  • D. Bone marrow failure: Not the primary described mortality mechanism for these enteric viral diseases.
  • B. Liver failure exclusively: Not the primary described mortality mechanism; dehydration/electrolyte imbalance from GI fluid loss is specifically emphasised.

posts.post_title: Colostrum Protection Against Neonatal Enteric Viruses
posts.post_content: Adequate colostrum intake helps protect neonates against rotavirus/coronavirus enteritis primarily by providing:

_aimcq_options.text: Direct antiviral drug compounds
Passive maternal antibodies (especially local intestinal IgA)
Only minerals with no immune role
Only fat-soluble vitamins with no immune role

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Colostrum provides passive maternal antibodies, especially local intestinal IgA, which coats the gut mucosa and provides important local protection against these enteric pathogens during the vulnerable early neonatal period.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Direct antiviral drug compounds: Incorrect — colostrum's protective effect is immunological (maternal antibody transfer), not pharmacological/drug-based.
  • D. Only fat-soluble vitamins with no immune role: Understates colostrum's key protective mechanism, which is centred on passive antibody transfer, not merely vitamin content.
  • C. Only minerals with no immune role: Understates colostrum's key protective mechanism, which is centred on passive antibody transfer, not merely mineral content.

posts.post_content: Neonatal diarrhoea outbreaks are often complicated by mixed infections because:

_aimcq_options.text: Bacterial infection always occurs first, followed by viral infection
Viral damage to the intestinal mucosa predisposes to secondary bacterial invasion (e.g. E. coli)
Mixed infections are extremely rare and clinically insignificant
Viruses and bacteria can never coexist in the same host

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Outbreaks are often complicated by mixed infections because viral damage to the intestinal mucosa predisposes to secondary bacterial invasion (e.g. enterotoxigenic E. coli), worsening overall disease severity and complicating diagnosis/treatment.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Viruses and bacteria can never coexist in the same host: Incorrect — concurrent viral-bacterial infection is a well-recognised and clinically important phenomenon in neonatal enteric disease.
  • A. Bacterial infection always occurs first, followed by viral infection: Not the typical/described sequence; viral mucosal damage is more commonly described as predisposing to secondary bacterial invasion, not the reverse order.
  • C. Mixed infections are extremely rare and clinically insignificant: Incorrect — mixed viral-bacterial neonatal enteritis is a recognised and clinically significant complicating factor in outbreak severity.

posts.post_content: Rotavirus is notable for being relatively:

_aimcq_options.text: Extremely fragile, destroyed instantly by any exposure to air
Only viable inside a living host cell with zero environmental survival
Completely eliminated by routine handwashing with plain water alone
Resistant to many common disinfectants, persisting in the environment

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rotavirus is relatively resistant to many common disinfectants and can persist in the environment for extended periods, contributing to its ability to cause recurring problems on breeding/calving premises if sanitation protocols aren't specifically effective against it.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Extremely fragile, destroyed instantly by any exposure to air: The opposite of the actual environmental resistance property described for rotavirus.
  • B. Only viable inside a living host cell with zero environmental survival: Incorrect — the virus's demonstrated environmental persistence contradicts a claim of zero survival outside host cells.
  • C. Completely eliminated by routine handwashing with plain water alone: Incorrect — its relative resistance to common disinfectants means it is not readily eliminated by simple water washing alone; targeted disinfection protocols are needed.

posts.post_content: Bacterial toxins released from within the cell wall upon bacterial death/lysis are termed:

_aimcq_options.text: Neurotoxins exclusively
Enterotoxins exclusively
Exotoxins
Endotoxins

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Endotoxins (lipopolysaccharide, LPS) are released upon lysis of gram-negative bacterial cell walls, causing systemic effects like fever, shock, and DIC.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Exotoxins: Actively secreted by living bacteria (e.g. Clostridium, Staphylococcus toxins), not released upon cell death/lysis.
  • B. Enterotoxins exclusively: A functional subcategory (targeting the gut) of exotoxins, not the general term for cell-wall-derived toxins released on lysis.
  • A. Neurotoxins exclusively: A functional subcategory (targeting nerves) of exotoxins, not the general term for cell-wall-derived toxins released on lysis.

posts.post_content: Chronic granulomatous inflammation, as seen in tuberculosis, is characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Only fibrin deposition with no cellular component
Epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and often central caseous necrosis
Only eosinophilic infiltration
Only acute neutrophilic infiltration

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Granulomatous inflammation is characterized by epithelioid macrophages, multinucleated giant cells (e.g. Langhans' type), and often central caseous necrosis, representing a chronic, organized immune response to persistent/poorly degradable antigens like mycobacteria.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Only acute neutrophilic infiltration: Describes acute/suppurative inflammation, not the chronic granulomatous pattern characteristic of tuberculosis.
  • C. Only eosinophilic infiltration: Not the characteristic cellular pattern of granulomatous inflammation; eosinophils are more associated with parasitic/allergic responses.
  • A. Only fibrin deposition with no cellular component: Describes fibrinous inflammation, a distinct pattern from the cellular (macrophage/giant cell) granulomatous response.

posts.post_content: Mycobacterium bovis, the cause of bovine tuberculosis, is notable for its:

_aimcq_options.text: Exclusively affecting birds
Strict host specificity limited only to cattle
Complete inability to infect any species besides cattle
Broad host range, including zoonotic transmission to humans

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

M. bovis has a broad host range, infecting cattle, wildlife reservoirs (e.g. badgers, deer, possums in various regions), and is zoonotic, historically an important cause of human TB via unpasteurised milk.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Strict host specificity limited only to cattle: Incorrect — the organism's broad host range (including wildlife and zoonotic potential to humans) is a defining epidemiological feature.
  • C. Complete inability to infect any species besides cattle: Incorrect — this contradicts the well-documented broad host range and zoonotic transmission.
  • A. Exclusively affecting birds: Incorrect — M. avium (not M. bovis) is the classic avian-associated mycobacterial species; M. bovis primarily affects cattle and other mammals.

posts.post_content: The tuberculin skin test detects prior mycobacterial exposure by measuring:

_aimcq_options.text: An immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity wheal
Bacterial culture growth directly from the skin
Antibody titre in serum only
A delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity response at the injection site

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The tuberculin test detects prior exposure by measuring a delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity response — a cell-mediated immune reaction causing localized swelling at the injection site, typically read 48-72 hours later.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. An immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity wheal: Incorrect — the tuberculin reaction is a delayed (Type IV), not immediate (Type I), hypersensitivity response, hence the 48-72 hour reading window rather than immediate assessment.
  • C. Antibody titre in serum only: Incorrect — the tuberculin test measures a cell-mediated (not antibody/humoral) response at the injection site, not a serum antibody titre.
  • B. Bacterial culture growth directly from the skin: Incorrect — the test is based on the host's immunological reaction to injected antigen, not direct bacterial culture from the skin.

posts.post_content: Johne's disease (paratuberculosis) is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Mycobacterium leprae
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Mycobacterium bovis
Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Johne's disease is caused by Mycobacterium avium subspecies paratuberculosis (MAP), causing chronic granulomatous enteritis with characteristic corrugated, thickened intestinal mucosa in ruminants.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Mycobacterium bovis: Causes bovine tuberculosis, a distinct disease from Johne's disease.
  • B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: The primary human TB agent, not the Johne's disease agent.
  • A. Mycobacterium leprae: The leprosy-causing agent (primarily in humans/armadillos), not the Johne's disease agent.

posts.post_content: The classic gross lesion of Johne's disease is:

_aimcq_options.text: Turkey-egg splenic infarcts
Diphtheritic pericarditis
Thickened, corrugated ("washboard") intestinal mucosa, especially the ileum
Copper-bronze liver

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Johne's disease shows the classic thickened, corrugated ("washboard") intestinal mucosa, especially affecting the ileum, reflecting chronic granulomatous inflammation and impaired nutrient absorption.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Copper-bronze liver: An avian fowl typhoid finding, not a Johne's disease lesion.
  • A. Turkey-egg splenic infarcts: A classical swine fever finding, not a Johne's disease lesion.
  • B. Diphtheritic pericarditis: Not a described Johne's disease finding; the disease centres on the intestinal tract.

posts.post_content: Mycobacterium species are characteristically demonstrated on histopathology/smears using:

_aimcq_options.text: Gram staining alone
Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) staining
Prussian blue staining
Congo red staining

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Mycobacteria are characteristically demonstrated using Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) staining, exploiting their waxy, mycolic-acid-rich cell wall that resists decolourisation by acid-alcohol.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Gram staining alone: Mycobacteria stain poorly/inconsistently with standard Gram stain due to their unique waxy cell wall; acid-fast staining is the specific method used.
  • C. Prussian blue staining: Used for haemosiderin (iron pigment) demonstration, not mycobacteria.
  • D. Congo red staining: Used for amyloid demonstration, not mycobacteria.

posts.post_content: Actinomycosis (Actinomyces bovis infection) in cattle is commonly known as:

_aimcq_options.text: Wooden tongue
Big head
Lumpy jaw
Blackleg

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Actinomycosis is commonly known as "lumpy jaw", reflecting the characteristic bony swelling of the mandible/maxilla caused by chronic granulomatous osteomyelitis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Wooden tongue: The common name for actinobacillosis (Actinobacillus lignieresii infection), affecting the tongue's soft tissue, a distinct but related condition.
  • B. Big head: The common name for Clostridium novyi type A infection in rams, an unrelated disease.
  • D. Blackleg: The common name for Clostridium chauvoei myonecrosis, an unrelated clostridial disease.

posts.post_content: Actinobacillosis (Actinobacillus lignieresii infection), commonly called "wooden tongue", primarily affects:

_aimcq_options.text: Only the lungs
Only the eyes
Soft tissue, especially the tongue
Only bone, especially the mandible

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Actinobacillosis ("wooden tongue") primarily affects soft tissue, especially the tongue, causing granulomatous glossitis with a characteristically firm, woody texture, unlike the bony involvement of actinomycosis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Only bone, especially the mandible: This describes actinomycosis ("lumpy jaw"), the bone-affecting counterpart condition, not actinobacillosis's soft-tissue tropism.
  • A. Only the lungs: Not the classic/primary site for actinobacillosis, which specifically affects the tongue/soft tissue.
  • B. Only the eyes: Not the classic/primary site for actinobacillosis.

posts.post_content: "Sulphur granules" seen grossly in actinomycotic/actinobacillotic lesions represent:

_aimcq_options.text: Actual elemental sulphur deposits
Calcified necrotic debris only
Fungal spore aggregates
Colonies of the causative filamentous bacteria surrounded by an eosinophilic (Splendore-Hoeppli) reaction

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

"Sulphur granules" are colonies of the causative filamentous bacteria surrounded by an eosinophilic (Splendore-Hoeppli) reaction — a club-like radiating pattern of antigen-antibody complexes, not actual sulphur.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Actual elemental sulphur deposits: A misnomer — despite the name, these granules do not contain elemental sulphur; they are bacterial colonies with a characteristic Splendore-Hoeppli reaction.
  • B. Calcified necrotic debris only: Not the correct description; these granules specifically represent bacterial colonies with the characteristic immune reaction, not simple calcified debris.
  • C. Fungal spore aggregates: Incorrect — while some fungal infections can show a similar Splendore-Hoeppli phenomenon, the classic "sulphur granules" of actinomycosis/actinobacillosis specifically represent bacterial colonies.

posts.post_content: Nocardia species, unlike Actinomyces, are characteristically:

_aimcq_options.text: Never found in soil
Unable to cause any pyogranulomatous disease
Obligate intracellular organisms
Partially acid-fast

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Nocardia species are characteristically partially acid-fast, a helpful distinguishing histochemical feature from Actinomyces species (which are not acid-fast), aiding differential diagnosis of these clinically similar filamentous bacterial infections.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Never found in soil: Incorrect — Nocardia species are actually soil saprophytes, an important epidemiological feature relevant to environmental exposure/wound contamination.
  • C. Obligate intracellular organisms: Incorrect — Nocardia are free-living environmental (soil) organisms, not obligate intracellular bacteria like Chlamydia.
  • B. Unable to cause any pyogranulomatous disease: Incorrect — Nocardia is a recognised cause of pyogranulomatous disease (e.g. nocardiosis affecting lungs, skin, other organs), similar in some respects to actinomycosis.

posts.post_content: Dermatophilosis ("rain scald", "lumpy wool") is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Actinomyces bovis
Dermatophilus congolensis
Nocardia asteroides
Actinobacillus lignieresii

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Dermatophilosis is caused by Dermatophilus congolensis, a filamentous actinomycete causing exudative dermatitis, classically associated with wet conditions ("rain scald" in horses, "lumpy wool" in sheep).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Actinomyces bovis: Causes actinomycosis ("lumpy jaw"), a distinct bone-affecting disease, not dermatophilosis.
  • C. Nocardia asteroides: Causes nocardiosis, a distinct pyogranulomatous disease pattern, not dermatophilosis.
  • D. Actinobacillus lignieresii: Causes actinobacillosis ("wooden tongue"), a distinct soft-tissue disease, not dermatophilosis.

posts.post_content: Dermatophilosis outbreaks are classically associated with:

_aimcq_options.text: Cold, dry winter conditions with no moisture
Excess dietary calcium
Extremely dry desert conditions
Prolonged wet weather/moisture exposure macerating the skin

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Outbreaks are classically associated with prolonged wet weather/moisture exposure, which macerates the skin and facilitates zoospore penetration by D. congolensis, explaining the disease's seasonal/climatic pattern.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Extremely dry desert conditions: The opposite of the actual predisposing factor — wet, not dry, conditions favour dermatophilosis development.
  • B. Excess dietary calcium: Not a described predisposing factor for dermatophilosis.
  • A. Cold, dry winter conditions with no moisture: Incorrect — the key predisposing factor is moisture/wet conditions, not dryness, regardless of temperature.

posts.post_content: Which feature helps distinguish actinomycosis (bone-invasive) from actinobacillosis (soft-tissue) clinically?

_aimcq_options.text: Actinobacillosis always causes bone destruction while actinomycosis never does
Actinomycosis characteristically causes bony swelling/osteomyelitis, while actinobacillosis affects soft tissue like the tongue
Both diseases are clinically and pathologically identical with no distinguishing features
Only actinomycosis is caused by a bacterium; actinobacillosis is viral

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

The key distinguishing clinical feature is that actinomycosis characteristically causes bony swelling/osteomyelitis ("lumpy jaw"), while actinobacillosis affects soft tissue, especially the tongue ("wooden tongue") — despite both being caused by related filamentous bacteria and sharing the "sulphur granule" histological feature.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. Actinobacillosis always causes bone destruction while actinomycosis never does: This reverses the actual pattern — bone involvement is characteristic of actinomycosis, not actinobacillosis, which is a soft-tissue disease.
  • C. Both diseases are clinically and pathologically identical with no distinguishing features: Incorrect — despite some overlapping features (sulphur granules), the tissue tropism (bone vs soft tissue) is a key clinical distinguishing feature.
  • D. Only actinomycosis is caused by a bacterium; actinobacillosis is viral: Incorrect — both actinomycosis and actinobacillosis are caused by bacteria (Actinomyces bovis and Actinobacillus lignieresii respectively), not one bacterial and one viral.

posts.post_content: Anthrax is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Bacillus anthracis
Clostridium septicum
Clostridium chauvoei
Clostridium novyi

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a spore-forming, gram-positive bacterium capable of forming highly resistant environmental spores.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • C. Clostridium chauvoei: The causative agent of blackleg (a clostridial myonecrosis), not anthrax.
  • B. Clostridium septicum: A causative agent of malignant oedema (a clostridial myonecrosis), not anthrax.
  • D. Clostridium novyi: A causative agent of "big head" and black disease (clostridial diseases), not anthrax.

posts.post_content: Full necropsy of an animal suspected to have died of anthrax is generally discouraged because:

_aimcq_options.text: The carcass poses no risk once death has occurred
The disease is not zoonotic, so no special precaution is needed
Anthrax cannot be diagnosed without full necropsy under any circumstances
Exposure to air causes B. anthracis to sporulate, creating highly resistant, long-lived environmental contamination

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Full necropsy is discouraged because exposure of the blood/tissues to air causes B. anthracis to sporulate, creating environmentally resistant spores that can persist in soil for decades, posing an ongoing infection risk to other animals/humans.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • A. The carcass poses no risk once death has occurred: Incorrect — this is precisely the danger; opening the carcass and exposing tissue to air triggers the sporulation that creates long-term environmental risk.
  • C. Anthrax cannot be diagnosed without full necropsy under any circumstances: Incorrect — anthrax can often be diagnosed via blood smear examination without full necropsy, precisely to avoid the sporulation risk.

  • C. Direct neurotoxin action with no vascular component: Incorrect — the vasculitis/thrombosis mechanism (not a direct neurotoxin) is specifically responsible for the multifocal brain lesions in TEME.
  • A. A purely nutritional deficiency with no infectious cause: Incorrect — TEME is fundamentally an infectious (H. somni) disease with a specific vasculitic pathogenesis, not a nutritional deficiency condition.
  • B. Prion-mediated neurodegeneration: Incorrect — TEME's mechanism is bacterial vasculitis/thrombosis, entirely distinct from prion disease pathogenesis.

posts.post_content: Diseases caused by Haemophilus-related organisms (Glaesserella parasuis, Histophilus somni) are classically associated with:

posts.post_content: Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae lesions in the lung typically show which distribution pattern?

posts.post_content: Haemophilus/Glaesserella species are notable for requiring which special growth factor for culture, reflecting the origin of the genus name?

posts.post_content: Mycoplasma species are unique among bacteria in that they lack:

_aimcq_options.text: A cell wall
The ability to replicate at all
Any cell membrane
Any genetic material

Correct Answer Explanation

Mycoplasma species are unique in lacking a cell wall, making them intrinsically resistant to beta-lactam antibiotics (which target cell wall synthesis) and giving them a pleomorphic appearance.

  • B. The ability to replicate at all: Incorrect — Mycoplasma species are capable of independent replication, unlike obligate intracellular organisms; their distinguishing feature is the absent cell wall, not an inability to replicate.
  • C. Any cell membrane: Incorrect — Mycoplasma does have a cell membrane; it specifically lacks the cell WALL, a distinct structure.

posts.post_content: Enzootic pneumonia in pigs, a chronic respiratory disease with major economic impact, is caused by:

posts.post_content: Contagious Bovine Pleuropneumonia (CBPP) is caused by:

posts.post_content: CBPP classically shows which distinctive gross lung lesion?

posts.post_content: Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia (CCPP), the goat counterpart to CBPP, is caused by:

posts.post_content: Because Mycoplasma species lack a cell wall, effective antibiotic treatment must avoid which class of drugs, which specifically target cell wall synthesis?

_aimcq_options.text: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins)
Fluoroquinolones
Macrolides
Tetracyclines

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Since Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall, beta-lactam antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins), which specifically target cell wall synthesis, are ineffective — tetracyclines, macrolides, and fluoroquinolones (which target other bacterial processes) are used instead.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Tetracyclines: Effective against Mycoplasma (targeting protein synthesis, not the cell wall), and are actually among the drugs of choice, not a class to avoid.
  • C. Macrolides: Effective against Mycoplasma (targeting protein synthesis), and are among the drugs of choice, not a class to avoid.
  • B. Fluoroquinolones: Effective against Mycoplasma (targeting DNA gyrase/topoisomerase, not the cell wall), and are a viable treatment option, not a class to avoid.

posts.post_content: Mycoplasmal respiratory diseases (e.g. enzootic pneumonia, CRD) are generally characterized by:

_aimcq_options.text: Complete absence of any economic significance
Chronic, slowly progressive disease with low mortality but significant economic impact via reduced growth/production
Instant, spontaneous full recovery with no economic consequence
Peracute disease with death within hours in nearly all cases

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Mycoplasmal respiratory diseases are generally characterized by a chronic, slowly progressive course with low mortality but significant economic impact via reduced growth rates, feed efficiency, and production — an important distinction from more acutely fatal bacterial respiratory pathogens.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Peracute disease with death within hours in nearly all cases: The opposite of the typical mycoplasmal disease pattern, which is chronic and low-mortality, not peracute and highly fatal (though CBPP/CCPP can be more severe exceptions within this general framework).
  • A. Complete absence of any economic significance: Incorrect — despite low mortality, the chronic production losses associated with these diseases represent major economic significance in affected industries.
  • C. Instant, spontaneous full recovery with no economic consequence: Incorrect — the chronic, persistent nature of these infections (and their associated production losses) is a defining and economically important feature, not spontaneous instant recovery.

posts.post_content: Rickettsial organisms (e.g. Anaplasma, Ehrlichia, Coxiella) are characterized by being:

_aimcq_options.text: Fungi
Viruses, not bacteria at all
Obligate intracellular bacteria
Free-living bacteria requiring no host cell

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

Rickettsial organisms are characterized as obligate intracellular bacteria, requiring a host cell for replication (unlike free-living bacteria), a feature they share conceptually with viruses despite being true bacteria with their own cellular machinery.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Free-living bacteria requiring no host cell: Incorrect — the defining feature of rickettsial organisms is specifically their OBLIGATE intracellular nature, requiring host cells, not free-living independence.
  • B. Viruses, not bacteria at all: Incorrect — despite their obligate intracellular lifestyle (superficially similar to viruses), rickettsial organisms are true bacteria, with their own ribosomes, cell wall, and independent metabolic machinery.
  • A. Fungi: Incorrect — rickettsial organisms are bacteria, not fungi.

posts.post_content: Bovine anaplasmosis is caused by:

_aimcq_options.text: Ehrlichia canis
Coxiella burnetii
Rickettsia rickettsii
Anaplasma marginale

Bovine anaplasmosis is caused by Anaplasma marginale, an intraerythrocytic rickettsial organism causing haemolytic anaemia, transmitted by ticks and mechanically by biting flies/contaminated instruments.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • B. Coxiella burnetii: The Q fever-causing organism, a distinct rickettsial disease from anaplasmosis.
  • A. Ehrlichia canis: The canine ehrlichiosis agent, a distinct organism/host from bovine anaplasmosis.

posts.post_content: Anaplasma marginale causes disease by:

Directly infecting bone exclusively
Directly infecting the brain exclusively

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer Explanation

A. marginale infects red blood cells, with infected RBCs subsequently recognised and removed by the spleen (extravascular haemolysis), leading to progressive haemolytic anaemia, icterus, and (in severe cases) death.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • D. Directly infecting the brain exclusively: Not the primary described mechanism/target of Anaplasma marginale, which specifically infects RBCs, not primarily the brain.
  • C. Directly infecting bone exclusively: Not the primary described mechanism/target of Anaplasma marginale.
  • A. Causing no cellular infection at all: Incorrect — RBC infection is precisely the defining pathogenic mechanism of this rickettsial organism.

posts.post_content: Q fever, a significant zoonosis particularly associated with reproductive tissues/fluids of livestock, is caused by:

  • A. Anaplasma marginale: The bovine anaplasmosis agent, a distinct organism and disease from Q fever.

posts.post_content: Chlamydia species, like Rickettsia, are characterized as:

posts.post_content: Superficial mycoses, as opposed to systemic mycoses, are characterized by infection primarily limited to:

The bloodstream exclusively

The central nervous system exclusively

posts.post_content: Ringworm (dermatophytosis) in domestic animals is most commonly caused by which two genera?

posts.post_content: Systemic/opportunistic fungal infections in animals are classically predisposed to by:

_aimcq_options.text: Only young, perfectly healthy animals
Excellent overall health with no other risk factors

Systemic/opportunistic mycoses are classically predisposed to by immunosuppression (from concurrent disease, prolonged antibiotic use disrupting normal flora, or corticosteroid/immunosuppressive therapy), allowing normally low-virulence environmental fungi to cause invasive disease.

  • B. Excellent overall health with no other risk factors: The opposite of the actual risk pattern — compromised, not excellent, host defence status is what predisposes to these opportunistic infections.

posts.post_content: Fungal culture for diagnostic purposes typically uses which type of selective media?

Blood agar exclusively
Tellurite agar
Sabouraud dextrose agar

posts.post_content: Special stains used to demonstrate fungal elements in tissue sections include:

  • B. Only Gram stain: Not the primary special stain used for fungal elements in tissue, which are better highlighted with PAS/GMS.

posts.post_content: Ringworm (dermatophytosis) is notable for being:

_aimcq_options.text: Never transmissible to humans under any circumstances
Exclusively a human disease with no animal reservoir
A disease that only affects internal organs
A recognised zoonosis, transmissible from animals to humans

posts.post_content: Coccidioides species are "dimorphic" fungi, meaning they exist as:

posts.post_content: Chronic, low-level aflatoxin exposure, even without acute clinical signs, can result in:

posts.post_content: A food-safety concern with aflatoxicosis in dairy animals is that:

posts.post_content: Confirming aflatoxicosis as the cause of clinical signs in a suspect herd/flock relies on:
